=== PAST LEARNINGS (from prior, independent episodes) ===
OPERATING PRINCIPLES (distilled from prior episodes in this run -- APPLY these now, don't just note them):
Keep doing:
  - Delegating a focused subtask with explicit instructions (try survival:cox with the observed_time sign-trick label, compare against binary:logistic baseline via lifelines concordance_index on held-out val.parquet, then retrain winner on full data) produced a clean, reproducible c-stat improvement from ~0.67 to ~0.684 — this comparison-then-retrain-on-full-data pattern is worth repeating.
  - Using pd.concat to assemble encoded feature columns (instead of iterative df[c]=... assignment) avoided the pandas fragmentation warning from prior episodes and is a cheap, low-risk fix worth keeping in any future finalize/model_def code.
  - Running a fresh-process sanity check (reload pickle, predict on val_features_only.parquet, assert shape/no-NaN/no-Inf, compute Harrell's C) caught no issues here and should remain standard practice before declaring the deliverable done.
  - Delegating the full train/validate/pickle pipeline to a subagent with an explicit, detailed spec (exclude leakage columns like grade/sub_grade/int_rate/installment, build model_def.py as a standalone class with self-contained feature prep, sanity-check via fresh-process reload) produced a clean, working deliverable with no errors.
  - Treating 'event' as a binary classification target (1=default, 0=censored) with xgboost binary:logistic and comparing against a logistic regression baseline is a simple, fast approach that clearly beat the baseline (0.67 vs 0.60 c-index) and is easy to verify.
  - Running an explicit sanity check (load pickle in fresh process, predict on val_features_only.parquet and holdout_features_only.parquet, check shape/NaN/Inf/range) caught no issues here and is a good practice to repeat since it would catch broken pickles or encoding bugs before submission.
Avoid repeating:
  - The categorical unseen-category encoding (map to -1) was still not explicitly stress-tested this episode (e.g. counting how many val/holdout rows fall back to -1 per column), so ep0000-neg1's concern remains unverified even though the same encoding scheme was reused again.
  - Hyperparameter tuning was limited to a small manual grid (4-5 combos) on a 200k-row subsample rather than a more systematic search or tuning on the full dataset, so there may still be unexplored gains from deeper/wider tuning of the cox objective (e.g. varying max_depth beyond 3-6, eta below 0.05, or num_boost_round beyond 400).
  - Only one modeling approach (plain binary:logistic XGBoost with default-ish hyperparameters, no tuning) and one baseline (plain logistic regression) were tried; no attempt at a proper survival objective (e.g. survival:cox using observed_time) or hyperparameter search was made, which may be leaving c-index on the table (~0.67 achieved).
  - Categorical encoding builds a fresh label map per column by iterating train uniques in arbitrary order and assigns -1 to unseen categories at inference, but this was never explicitly stress-tested against holdout rows with categories absent from train to confirm it doesn't degrade predictions for a meaningful fraction of rows.
  - The per-column loop building the output DataFrame (inserting columns one at a time via out[c]=...) triggers a pandas 'highly fragmented frame' warning, indicating inefficient code that could be slow on larger datasets; using pd.concat for column assembly would be more robust/performant for scaling up feature engineering.

Identify the single strongest prior approach and describe it now.

input.recommended_approach: Train an XGBoost survival model using the 'survival:cox' objective, with the label constructed via the standard "sign-trick" encoding of (observed_time, event) — i.e., label = observed_time if event==1 (default/uncensored) else -observed_time if event==0 (censored), as required by XGBoost's Cox partial likelihood loss. Build features by excluding obvious leakage columns (grade, sub_grade, int_rate, installment, and any other fields directly derived from the outcome/pricing decision), encoding categoricals via per-column label maps (built from train uniques) with unseen categories at inference mapped to -1. Assemble the engineered feature DataFrame using pd.concat (not iterative df[c]=... assignment) to avoid fragmentation warnings/slowness. Train on the full training set, and compare against a binary:logistic XGBoost baseline (treating 'event' as the binary target) and a logistic regression baseline, evaluating all candidates with Harrell's concordance index (lifelines concordance_index) on held-out val.parquet. Pick the winner (Cox model beat binary logistic: ~0.684 vs ~0.67 c-index, both beating logistic regression baseline ~0.60), then retrain that winning configuration on the full dataset (train+val) before finalizing. Package the final model as a standalone model_def.py class with self-contained feature preprocessing, pickle it, and do a fresh-process sanity check: reload the pickle, predict on val_features_only.parquet and holdout_features_only.parquet, and assert correct shape, no NaN/Inf, and sane score range.
input.rationale: Across the reported episodes, this was the only approach that explicitly beat the straightforward binary classification baseline on the stated validation metric (c-index ~0.684 vs ~0.67 for binary:logistic XGBoost vs ~0.60 for logistic regression). It is concrete (specific objective, label construction trick, leakage-column exclusions, encoding scheme) and was validated with a reproducible train/compare/retrain-on-full-data/sanity-check pipeline, which the learnings repeatedly flag as a good practice to retain. It also surfaces known unresolved risks (unseen-category encoding, limited hyperparameter search) that the new agent should keep in mind as potential further improvements rather than blockers.
